title: Norse Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Old Norse pantheon mapped as a relationship graph: the giants and the making of the world from Ymir's body, the Aesir and the Vanir, the nine worlds on Yggdrasil, and the fixed road to Ragnarok.
sources: The Poetic Edda, translated by Henry Adams Bellows (1936)
Snorri Sturluson, The Prose Edda, translated by Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur (1916)
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, translated by Samuel Laing (1844)
The Volsunga Saga, translated by Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris (1888)
Saxo Grammaticus, The Danish History, translated by Oliver Elton (1894)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia for cross-checking manuscript attestation
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/norse/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

profile.cosmicNature: Linear, with a known ending. The world is built from the body of a murdered giant, runs its course, and is destroyed at Ragnarok in a battle whose participants and outcome are already fixed. A new green earth rises afterwards and a few survivors return, but the tradition puts almost all its weight on the ending rather than the renewal.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Mortal. The Aesir are stronger and longer-lived than men but they can be killed, they need Idunn's apples to stay young, and they know in detail how and by whom each of them will die. They are not creators of the moral order and are not omniscient; Odin spends the whole tradition trying to buy information he does not have, at increasing cost.
profile.afterlife: Divided by how you die rather than how you lived. Half the battle-slain go to Odin's Valhalla and half to Freyja's Folkvangr; the drowned go to Ran's hall under the sea; everyone else goes to Hel, which is not a punishment, merely dim. There is no judgment and no weighing - a bad man and a good man who die in bed arrive at the same place.
profile.systemMechanism: Fate outranks the gods. The Norns carve what will happen at the roots of the world tree, and neither Odin's knowledge nor Thor's strength alters it; Odin gathers warriors for a battle he knows he loses. What the tradition values is not escape but conduct - knowing the ending and going to meet it anyway, which is the nearest thing Norse religion has to a doctrine.
profile.canonTexts: The Poetic Edda, an anonymous collection of older verse; Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda of about 1220; Heimskringla; the legendary and family sagas, above all the Volsunga Saga; and Saxo Grammaticus' Latin Gesta Danorum.

entities.name: Ymir
entities.role: The first giant, from whose body the world was made
domains: the raw material of the world
entities.abode: Ginnungagap, before there was anywhere else
entities.bio: The first living thing, formed from meeting rime and fire, and killed by Odin and his brothers to build the world.
entities.longBio: In the beginning there is Ginnungagap, the yawning gap, with the ice of Niflheim to the north and the fire of Muspelheim to the south. Where they meet the rime drips and quickens into Ymir, who sleeps and sweats, and from his left armpit a man and woman grow while his legs beget a son on each other - the frost-giants descend from him. He is fed by the cow Audhumla, who licks a salted rime-block until Buri emerges from it. Buri's grandsons Odin, Vili and Ve kill Ymir, and so much blood pours out that all the frost-giants drown but two. The three make the world from the corpse: earth from his flesh, mountains from his bones, sea from his blood, the sky from his skull held up by four dwarfs, and clouds from his brains.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri gives the fullest account and reconciles verse sources that disagree; the Poetic Edda's Vafthrudnismal calls the first being Aurgelmir, and whether that is another name for Ymir is Snorri's inference.

entities.name: Audhumla
entities.role: The primeval cow
domains: nourishment before there was anything to eat
the licking free of the first god
entities.bio: The cow who fed Ymir with four rivers of milk and licked Buri out of the salty ice.
entities.longBio: Audhumla comes into being from the melting rime at the same moment as Ymir, and the arrangement is simple and strange: four rivers of milk run from her udders and Ymir drinks, and she herself feeds by licking salty rime-blocks. Over three days her licking uncovers a man in the ice - first his hair, then his head, then all of him. This is Buri, the first of the gods, whose son Bor fathers Odin, Vili and Ve on the giantess Bestla. So the entire divine line is licked out of ice by a cow, and the entire giant line is fed by her milk, which makes Audhumla the common origin of both sides of the war that runs through the whole mythology. She then disappears from the record entirely.
entities.variantTraditions: Audhumla appears only in Snorri; no surviving eddic poem mentions her, so she may be his own material or from a source now lost.

entities.name: Odin
entities.role: All-father; god of poetry, war, wisdom and the dead
festivals: Yule, associated with the Wild Hunt
entities.worship: Worshipped chiefly by kings, poets and warriors rather than farmers, with a grim reputation: sacrifices to him included hanging, and Adam of Bremen describes the nine-yearly offerings at Uppsala.
entities.bio: One-eyed seeker who trades an eye and hangs himself to buy knowledge, and gathers the slain for a battle he knows he loses.
entities.longBio: Odin is not a comfortable king. What defines him is appetite for knowledge and willingness to pay: he gives an eye to Mimir for a drink from the well beneath the world tree, and hangs himself on that tree, pierced by his own spear, nine nights, given to himself, to seize the runes. He steals the mead of poetry from the giants by seduction and deceit. He goes disguised through the world under dozens of names, testing men and losing riddle contests on purpose to learn what his opponent knows. His ravens Huginn and Muninn, thought and memory, fly out daily and report. He gathers half the battle-slain to Valhalla to fight beside him at Ragnarok, where Fenrir will swallow him - and he knows this, in detail, and does it anyway. He is also a repeated oath-breaker, which the sources state without apology.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri's euhemerising Heimskringla makes Odin a human king from Asia who was later mistaken for a god - a Christian rationalisation, not a Norse belief. Saxo is likewise hostile to him.

entities.name: Thor
entities.role: God of thunder and defender of the world
domains: the defence of gods and men against giants
festivals: Midwinter blot; Thursday carries his name
entities.worship: The most broadly worshipped god of the Viking age. Hammer amulets were worn in enormous numbers, and Icelandic settlers named more places and children after him than after any other god.
entities.bio: Red-bearded thunder god whose hammer keeps the giants out; the most widely worshipped of the Norse gods.
entities.longBio: Thor is the god ordinary people actually prayed to. Where Odin's constituency is kings and poets, Thor's is farmers and sailors, and hammer amulets outnumber every other identifiable religious object from the Viking age. His function is defence: he keeps the giants from overrunning the world, and he does it by direct application of force. His hammer Mjollnir always returns when thrown, and it hallows as well as kills - it is raised over a bride at weddings and over the newborn. His adventures are physical and often comic: fishing for the world serpent with an ox head, wrestling an old woman who turns out to be old age, having his hammer stolen and being obliged to dress as a bride to recover it, a story the tradition finds hilarious rather than shameful. At Ragnarok he kills Jormungandr and walks nine paces before the venom drops him.
entities.variantTraditions: Thor's chariot is drawn by two goats he can slaughter and revive, provided the bones are unbroken; a farm boy who splits one for marrow becomes his servant.

entities.name: Frigg
entities.role: Queen of the Aesir; she who knows all fates and says nothing
entities.bio: Odin's wife, who knows every fate but never speaks it, and whose attempt to save her son fails on one detail.
entities.longBio: Frigg is said to know all fates though she tells no one, which puts her in an unusual position: she is the only figure in the tradition who has Odin's knowledge without his hunger for it. She sits at Fensalir and spins. Her great act is the attempt to save Baldr: warned by his dreams, she travels the whole world exacting an oath from every thing - fire, water, iron, stone, beasts, birds, sickness, poison - that it will not harm him, and she succeeds completely except for one young mistletoe west of Valhalla that she judges too small to bother with. Loki learns this by wheedling it out of her in disguise, and that single omission kills her son. Afterwards she asks who will ride to Hel to ransom him. She and Odin also appear wagering over the fates of two mortal kings, each cheating to win.
entities.variantTraditions: Frigg and Freyja overlap enough - both associated with love, both with falcon-feathers - that they may descend from one earlier goddess; Old High German sources and the Friday naming complicate the picture further.

entities.name: Loki
entities.role: The trickster; blood-brother of Odin and enemy of the gods
domains: the causing and solving of trouble
entities.abode: Asgard, until he is bound beneath the earth
entities.bio: A giant who lives among the gods, causes most of their problems, solves most of them, and finally kills Baldr.
entities.longBio: Loki is a giant by birth and Odin's sworn blood-brother by oath, which is why the Aesir tolerate him. The pattern is nearly always the same: he creates a crisis by malice or carelessness, and is then forced on pain of death to fix it, and the fixing produces something valuable - Sif's golden hair, Odin's spear, Thor's hammer, Freyr's ship and boar, and Odin's eight-legged horse, which Loki bears himself after turning into a mare. He is genuinely funny and genuinely dangerous, and the tradition never resolves which. The turn comes with Baldr: he finds the one thing that has not sworn, guides the blind Hodr's hand, and then blocks the ransom from Hel. For that he is bound with his own son's entrails beneath a dripping serpent until Ragnarok, when he breaks free and steers the ship of the dead against the gods.
entities.variantTraditions: How much of Loki's demonic final character is Christian colouring in Snorri is much argued; the eddic poem Lokasenna already shows him as an insulting outsider, but the parallels drawn with Satan are modern.

entities.name: Baldr
entities.role: The bright god, killed by mistletoe
domains: the loss that cannot be undone
entities.bio: Son of Odin and Frigg, so beloved that everything swore not to harm him, killed by the one thing that did not.
entities.longBio: Baldr is the best of the gods and the one whose death matters most, because it is the first irreversible thing to happen to them and the beginning of the end. Troubled by dreams of his own death, he tells the Aesir; Frigg extracts oaths from everything, after which the gods amuse themselves by throwing weapons at him and watching them refuse to bite. Loki, disguised as a woman, learns of the overlooked mistletoe, makes a dart of it, and puts it in the hand of Baldr's blind brother Hodr, guiding the throw. Baldr dies. Hermod rides nine nights to Hel, who agrees to release him if every thing in the world weeps - and every thing does, except one giantess in a cave who will not, and who is generally taken to be Loki. Baldr stays dead until after Ragnarok, when he returns to the new world.
entities.variantTraditions: Saxo tells a completely different and more human version in which Balderus and Hotherus are rivals for a woman and fight a straightforward war; the two accounts cannot be reconciled.

entities.name: Hodr
entities.role: The blind god who threw the dart
entities.bio: Baldr's blind brother, who killed him without knowing and was killed in revenge within a day.
entities.longBio: Hodr is blind and is standing outside the ring of gods amusing themselves with Baldr's invulnerability, because he cannot see to join in and has no weapon. Loki asks why he is not honouring Baldr like the others, offers to direct him, and puts the mistletoe in his hand. He throws, and Baldr falls dead. The Aesir cannot take vengeance in the sanctuary where they stand, so Odin fathers a son, Vali, on the giantess Rind expressly for the purpose; Vali is one night old when he kills Hodr. Hodr and Baldr both return after Ragnarok and live in the new world together, which is one of the few notes of reconciliation the tradition permits itself.
entities.variantTraditions: Saxo's Hotherus is not blind and not innocent but a rival warrior who kills Balderus in open contest; the two versions are irreconcilable.

entities.name: Tyr
entities.role: God of law and of the sacrificed hand
entities.worship: Tuesday carries his name. He was invoked in matters of law and in the duel, and the Tiwaz rune was carved on weapons for victory.
entities.bio: God of law who put his hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge, knowing he would lose it.
entities.longBio: Tyr's defining act is a deliberate loss. The gods want to bind the wolf Fenrir with the fetter Gleipnir, and the wolf, suspicious, will only allow it if one of them puts a hand in his mouth as surety of good faith. Every god refuses except Tyr. The fetter holds, the wolf cannot break it, and he bites the hand off at the wrist - and the sources are clear that Tyr knew this would happen, which is what makes it a pledge rather than a gamble. That single episode carries the whole character: he is the god of the oath and of the legal assembly, and he pays what an oath costs. Linguistic evidence suggests he was once far more important, since his name descends from the same root as Zeus and Jupiter and simply means god, which usually indicates an older sky-father displaced by later arrivals.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tyr of the surviving myths is much reduced from what the etymology implies; the Germanic Tiwaz appears to have been a chief deity before Odin's rise.

entities.name: Heimdall
entities.role: Watchman of the gods
domains: the founding of the social orders
entities.abode: Himinbjorg, at the end of Bifrost
entities.bio: The watchman who needs less sleep than a bird, hears grass grow, and will blow the horn at Ragnarok.
entities.longBio: Heimdall sits at the end of the rainbow bridge and watches. He requires less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and can hear wool growing on a sheep and grass growing on the earth; his horn Gjallarhorn is heard through all the worlds, and he will sound it when the giants come. He was born of nine mothers, generally taken to be the nine daughters of the sea, which is not explained anywhere. In the poem Rigsthula he walks among men under the name Rig, fathering the three social classes - thrall, farmer and lord - on three couples, which makes him the origin of human society as the Norse understood it. He and Loki are enemies from the start, they once fought in the shape of seals over a necklace, and at Ragnarok they kill each other.
entities.variantTraditions: Rigsthula's attribution of Rig to Heimdall rests on a prose header that may be a later addition; some scholars read the poem's Rig as Odin.

entities.name: Bragi
entities.role: God of poetry
domains: the welcoming of the slain to Valhalla
entities.bio: Skald of the gods, husband of Idunn, who greets the dead arriving at Valhalla.
entities.longBio: Bragi is wise in poetry above all others, with runes cut on his tongue, and the word bragr in Old Norse means poetry itself, so it is genuinely unclear whether the god gave his name to the art or the art was personified into a god. He greets the einherjar as they arrive in Valhalla. He is married to Idunn, who keeps the apples of youth. In Lokasenna, when Loki forces his way into the gods' hall and insults everyone in turn, Bragi is the first to try to bar him and gets the worst of the exchange, being told he is brave on his bench and no use in a fight. There is also a historical Bragi Boddason, a ninth-century Norwegian poet and the earliest skald whose verse survives, and the relationship between the man and the god is unresolved.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether the god Bragi derives from the historical poet Bragi Boddason, or the reverse, has been argued both ways since the nineteenth century.

entities.name: Idunn
entities.role: Keeper of the apples of youth
domains: the apples that keep the gods from ageing
entities.bio: The goddess whose apples keep the gods young, and whose abduction nearly ends them.
entities.longBio: The Aesir are not immortal by nature; they stay young by eating Idunn's apples, which she keeps in an ash box and distributes. That makes her the single point of failure in the whole divine order, and the tradition exploits it. Loki, under duress from the giant Thjazi, lures her out of Asgard with a story about better apples growing in a wood nearby, and Thjazi in eagle shape carries her off. The gods immediately begin to grey and stiffen, work out who was last seen with her, and give Loki the obvious choice. He borrows Freyja's falcon cloak, flies to Thrymheim, turns Idunn into a nut and carries her home with Thjazi in pursuit; the giant burns his wings on fires the gods light along the walls and is killed as he falls.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri's account is the fullest; the poem Haustlong describes the same episode in kennings and is the older source.

entities.name: Sif
entities.role: Golden-haired wife of Thor
domains: the household of the thunder god
entities.bio: Thor's wife, whose hair Loki cut off, and whose replacement hair produced the gods' greatest treasures.
entities.longBio: Sif is chiefly remembered for her hair, and for what happened when Loki cut it off while she slept - a piece of pure malice with no motive given. Thor's response is to threaten to break every bone in Loki's body unless he replaces it, and Loki goes to the dwarfs. The sons of Ivaldi make hair of real gold that grows like hair, and while he is there Loki provokes a wager between two sets of dwarfs that produces, in the same session, Odin's spear Gungnir, Freyr's collapsible ship Skidbladnir, Odin's ring Draupnir, Freyr's golden boar, and Thor's hammer Mjollnir - short in the handle because Loki, in fly shape, bit the dwarf working the bellows. So the gods' entire arsenal exists because of a haircut. Sif's golden hair is generally read as ripe grain, making her a harvest figure.
entities.variantTraditions: Sif is barely characterised outside this story; Loki in Lokasenna claims to have been her lover, which she does not deny.

entities.name: Njord
entities.role: God of the sea, wind and wealth
entities.abode: Noatun, the ship-enclosure by the shore
entities.worship: Invoked by fishermen and traders. Icelandic oaths were sworn by Njord and Freyr, and place-names in Norway and Sweden preserve his cult.
entities.bio: Vanir god of sea and wealth, sent to the Aesir as a hostage, whose marriage failed over where to live.
entities.longBio: Njord comes to the Aesir as a hostage at the end of the Aesir-Vanir war and stays. His domain is the profitable sea rather than the dangerous one: fair winds, good catches, safe voyages, and the wealth they bring, and he was invoked for prosperity as much as for weather. His marriage to the giantess Skadi is one of the tradition's better jokes about incompatibility. She chose him by looking only at feet, expecting Baldr; they agreed to live nine nights in her mountains and nine at his shore, and each hated the other's home - he could not stand the wolves howling in the hills, she could not stand the gulls waking her at the sea. They separated. His children Freyr and Freyja were born before he joined the Aesir, to his own sister, a Vanir practice the Aesir did not permit.
entities.variantTraditions: Njord's name descends from the same root as Nerthus, a goddess Tacitus describes among Germanic tribes in the first century, suggesting a change of sex somewhere in a thousand years of transmission.

entities.name: Freyr
entities.role: God of fertility, peace and good harvest
entities.abode: Alfheim, given to him as a teething gift
festivals: Harvest blot; the Swedish kings claimed descent from him
entities.worship: Central to Swedish cult at Uppsala. Oaths were sworn on the Freyr boar, and his image was carried through the countryside in a wagon to bless the fields.
entities.bio: The most beloved of the Vanir, who traded away the sword he will need at Ragnarok for a giantess.
entities.longBio: Freyr governs everything that makes life possible rather than glorious: rain, sun, the harvest, peace and prosperity. He owns Skidbladnir, a ship that always has a fair wind and folds into a pouch, and the golden boar Gullinbursti that runs on air and water and lights the night. His central story is a bad bargain. Sitting on Odin's high seat he sees the giantess Gerdr, is stricken, and sends his servant Skirnir to woo her; Skirnir wins her only after threats of appalling curses, and the fee Freyr pays is his own sword, which fights by itself. He gets Gerdr. At Ragnarok he faces the fire-giant Surtr without it and dies, and the tradition is explicit that this is the price of that afternoon.
entities.variantTraditions: Adam of Bremen describes an image of Fricco at Uppsala with an enormous phallus, generally identified with Freyr; the Ynglinga saga makes him a human king of the Swedes, euhemerised.

entities.name: Freyja
entities.role: Goddess of love, fertility, war, gold and seidr
domains: war and the choosing of the slain
entities.worship: Widely invoked in matters of love and childbirth. Late medieval Scandinavian records show her name surviving in charms long after conversion.
entities.bio: The most requested goddess in the tradition: she takes half the battle-slain, teaches the gods magic, and weeps gold.
entities.longBio: Freyja is the strongest and least domesticated of the goddesses. She takes half of everyone who falls in battle - Odin gets the other half, and the sources note that she chooses first. She taught seidr, the shape-shifting, fate-altering magic, to the Aesir including Odin, which makes her his teacher in the one area he most values. She drives a chariot drawn by cats, owns a falcon cloak the other gods borrow, and weeps tears of red gold for her wandering husband Odr. Her necklace Brisingamen she bought from four dwarfs at a price the sources name plainly. Every giant who wants something demands Freyja: the builder of Asgard's wall, Thrym who steals Thor's hammer, Hrungnir. The gods never seriously consider it, but the pattern says what she is worth.
entities.variantTraditions: Freyja and Frigg overlap enough that many scholars suspect one earlier goddess; Snorri keeps them separate, and Old High German evidence complicates the case.

entities.name: Kvasir
entities.role: The wisest being, made from spittle and murdered for his blood
entities.bio: Formed from the spittle of both god-tribes at their truce, and killed by dwarfs to brew the mead of poetry.
entities.longBio: When the Aesir and Vanir made peace they sealed it by all spitting into one vat, and from that spittle they formed Kvasir, who knew the answer to every question asked of him. He travelled the world teaching. Two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, invited him in and killed him, telling the gods he had choked on his own wisdom because no one was learned enough to ask him anything. They mixed his blood with honey and brewed the mead of poetry, which makes whoever drinks it a poet or a scholar. The mead then passed by murder and extortion to the giant Suttung, and Odin stole it in turn. So poetry in Norse terms descends from a peace treaty, a murder and a theft, which the tradition presents entirely without embarrassment.
entities.variantTraditions: Kvasir's name may be related to a word for crushed fruit or fermented drink, which would make him a personification of the mead rather than its source.

entities.name: Vidar
entities.role: The silent god who avenges Odin
symbols: the thick shoe made of scrap leather
entities.abode: Vidi, a land of brushwood and high grass
entities.bio: Second strongest of the gods, who kills Fenrir at Ragnarok and lives to see the new world.
entities.longBio: Vidar barely speaks and barely appears until the end, which is the point: he is kept in reserve. He wears one enormously thick shoe made from every scrap of leather ever trimmed from a shoe's toe and heel and discarded, saved up across all of human history for one purpose. At Ragnarok, when Fenrir has swallowed Odin, Vidar steps into the wolf's lower jaw with that shoe, takes hold of the upper jaw, and tears the mouth apart. He is one of the handful who survive the burning and return to the new green earth with Baldr and Hodr. He is called the silent god, and the sources give no reason, which has led to a lot of speculation about ritual silence in vengeance that the texts themselves do not support.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri's detail about the shoe includes an instruction to cobblers to discard those trimmings if they wish to help the gods, which may be his own embroidery.

entities.name: Vali
entities.role: Born to avenge Baldr, and one night old when he did
entities.bio: Odin fathered him on a giantess expressly to kill Hodr, which he did at one night old.
entities.longBio: The Aesir cannot avenge Baldr where they stand, because the place is sanctuary and blood may not be shed there. Odin's answer is procedural and cold: he fathers a son on the giantess Rind for the single purpose of vengeance. Vali is born, grows to full strength in a day, and kills Hodr when he is one night old, having neither washed his hands nor combed his hair - details the poem gives to mark that he does nothing else first. He then has no further part in anything until Ragnarok, which he survives, returning to the new world with Vidar and Baldr and Hodr. Saxo tells a much longer version in which Odin's wooing of Rind involves three rejections, disguise as a woman and something close to assault.
entities.variantTraditions: Saxo's account of the wooing of Rinda is far more disreputable than Snorri's and was probably meant to discredit Odin.

entities.name: Ullr
entities.role: God of the bow, the ski and the shield
entities.bio: Archer and skier, invoked in duels, and once important enough to be worth swearing by.
entities.longBio: Ullr has almost no surviving mythology and an enormous number of place-names, which is a reliable sign of a god who mattered far more than the texts admit. He is Sif's son and Thor's stepson, lives in the yew-dales - yew being the bow-wood - and travels on skis with a bow. His shield could be used as a boat, and the poets' word for a shield is Ullr's ship. Men in a duel called on him, and an eddic verse mentions swearing an oath on Ullr's ring, a formula that implies real cultic weight. Saxo has a figure named Ollerus rule in Odin's place during a ten-year exile and cross the sea on a bone inscribed with spells, which sounds like a fragment of a much larger lost tradition.
entities.variantTraditions: The mismatch between Ullr's place-name density in Norway and Sweden and his near-absence from the myths is one of the clearest signs of how much has been lost.

entities.name: Forseti
entities.role: God of judgment and reconciliation
entities.abode: Glitnir, with pillars of gold and a roof of silver
entities.bio: Son of Baldr, who sits in a golden hall and settles every dispute brought to him.
entities.longBio: Forseti's name means the one who presides, which is the ordinary Old Norse word for the chairman of an assembly and is still the modern Icelandic word for president. He is the son of Baldr and Nanna, and he lives in Glitnir, a hall on pillars of gold with a silver roof that can be seen a long way off. All who come to him with a dispute leave reconciled; the sources say he is the best of judges and that no one leaves his court unsatisfied, which is a striking claim in a legal culture built on feud. A medieval Frisian legend tells of a lawgiver named Fosite who appeared in a boat of twelve men and gave them their law, and the Frisian island Heligoland was called Fositesland.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between the Norse Forseti and the Frisian Fosite is disputed - shared origin, borrowing, or coincidence of names.

entities.name: Hermod
entities.role: The messenger who rode to Hel
entities.bio: Odin's son, who rode nine nights down to Hel to ransom Baldr and nearly succeeded.
entities.longBio: When Baldr is dead and Frigg asks who will ride to Hel and offer a ransom, Hermod volunteers. He borrows Sleipnir and rides nine nights through valleys so dark he sees nothing until he reaches the river Gjoll and its gold-roofed bridge, where the maiden guarding it remarks that he does not have the colour of a dead man. He jumps the gate of Hel outright and finds Baldr sitting in the seat of honour. Hel agrees to release him on one condition: that every thing in the world, living and dead, weep for him. Hermod rides back with the answer and with Draupnir, and the gods send word everywhere, and everything weeps - except one giantess in a cave who says she will weep dry tears and that Hel may keep what she has.
entities.variantTraditions: Hermod appears almost nowhere else; whether he was an established god or a figure Snorri needed for this errand is unclear.

entities.name: Nanna
entities.role: Baldr's wife, who died of grief at his pyre
entities.bio: She died of grief as Baldr's body was carried to the pyre, and was burned beside him.
entities.longBio: Nanna's part is short and complete. As Baldr's body is being placed on the ship Hringhorni for burning, she sees it, her heart breaks, and she dies on the spot; she is laid on the pyre beside him. When Hermod reaches Hel he finds them both there, and Nanna sends gifts back to the living - a linen robe for Frigg and a gold ring for Fulla - which is a small domestic gesture in the middle of the tradition's largest catastrophe and lands harder for it. Their son Forseti becomes the god of reconciliation, which reads as the tradition's one attempt to get something constructive out of the whole affair. In Saxo she is an entirely different character, a mortal woman who rejects Balderus for Hotherus and is the cause of their war.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri's Nanna dies of grief; Saxo's Nanna is the living object of a rivalry. The two share nothing but a name.

entities.name: Sigyn
entities.role: Loki's wife, who holds the bowl
entities.abode: The cave where Loki is bound
entities.bio: She catches the venom dripping on her bound husband, and the earth shakes when she turns to empty the bowl.
entities.longBio: After Loki is caught, the gods turn one of his sons into a wolf, which tears the other apart, and bind Loki to three stones with his son's entrails, which harden into iron. Skadi fixes a serpent above his face to drip venom onto him. Sigyn stays. She holds a basin under the serpent to catch the venom, and Loki is unharmed - until the basin fills and she must turn away to empty it, and the drops fall on his face and he writhes so hard that the whole earth shakes, which is what earthquakes are. Then she comes back and holds the bowl again. She does this until Ragnarok. She has no other story, no lineage of note and almost no lines, and she is one of the most affecting figures in the corpus.
entities.variantTraditions: Sigyn appears in the Poetic Edda and in Snorri; nothing is said about why she stays.

entities.name: Gefjon
entities.role: Who ploughed Zealand out of Sweden
entities.bio: She turned her four sons into oxen and ploughed an island out of Sweden in a night.
entities.longBio: King Gylfi of Sweden offered Gefjon as much land as she could plough in a day and a night. She went to Jotunheim, bore four sons to a giant, turned them into oxen, and set them to a plough that cut so deep it tore the land loose and dragged it west into the sea, where it became Zealand; the hole left behind filled with water and became lake Malaren, whose bays are said to match the island's headlands. Snorri notes that she is served by all women who die unmarried, which makes her the counterpart to the goddesses who receive wives and mothers. In Lokasenna, Loki accuses her of having taken a necklace for sex, an accusation he makes about most of the goddesses present.
entities.variantTraditions: Snorri opens Gylfaginning with this story and repeats it in Heimskringla with a poem by Bragi as evidence, which is unusually good attestation by his standards.

entities.name: Skadi
entities.role: Giantess of the mountains, ski and bow
entities.bio: She came to Asgard armed to avenge her father and left with a husband, a settlement, and a place among the gods.
entities.longBio: Skadi's father Thjazi is killed by the Aesir after the theft of Idunn, and she arrives at Asgard in mail with a drawn bow to take vengeance. The gods offer settlement instead: she may choose a husband from among them, but only by looking at their feet. She picks the finest pair expecting Baldr and gets Njord. She further requires that they make her laugh, which no one can until Loki ties a rope from his testicles to a goat's beard and the resulting contest ends with him falling in her lap. She laughs. The marriage fails on geography and they separate; she goes back to the mountains and her skis. She is the one who fixes the serpent above the bound Loki, which reads as a long-deferred settling of accounts.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ynglinga saga has her later marry Odin and bear him many sons; the sources do not agree about where she ends up.

entities.name: Gerdr
entities.role: The giantess whose arms lit the sky
symbols: arms that light air and water
entities.bio: Freyr saw her from Odin's high seat and paid his sword for her; she agreed only under threat of curses.
entities.longBio: When Freyr sits in the forbidden high seat and looks out over all worlds, he sees a woman go into a house, and the light of her arms shines on the sky and the sea. He becomes ill with longing and will not eat or speak. His servant Skirnir is sent to woo her and takes Freyr's self-fighting sword as his fee. Gerdr refuses gold and apples flatly; she yields only when Skirnir threatens her with a rune-carved curse of madness, monstrous marriage and endless unsatisfied desire. She agrees to meet Freyr in nine nights. Scholars have read the whole episode as a fertility rite - the sky god's light compelling the frozen field - but the poem as it stands is a coercion, and it costs Freyr his life at Ragnarok.
entities.variantTraditions: The fertility-rite reading of Skirnismal is influential but contested; the text itself presents a straightforward threat.

entities.name: Thjazi
entities.role: The eagle-giant who stole Idunn
entities.bio: He forced Loki to deliver Idunn and her apples, and burned to death chasing them home.
entities.longBio: Thjazi first appears as an eagle who settles on an ox the gods are cooking and prevents it from roasting until he is given a share, then takes most of it. Loki strikes at him with a pole, which sticks fast, and Thjazi flies off with Loki attached and dragging until he agrees to bring him Idunn. Loki lures her out of Asgard and Thjazi carries her to Thrymheim. The gods begin to age at once, work out who is responsible, and send Loki to fix it. He takes Freyja's falcon cloak, turns Idunn into a nut, and flies; Thjazi follows in eagle shape and burns his wings on fires the gods have set along the walls of Asgard, and is killed inside. Odin throws his eyes into the sky as stars.
entities.variantTraditions: The story survives in Snorri and in the older skaldic poem Haustlong, which describes it in dense kennings on a painted shield.

entities.name: Thrym
entities.role: The giant who stole Thor's hammer
entities.bio: He hid Mjollnir eight leagues underground and demanded Freyja as the price, and was killed at his own wedding.
entities.longBio: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone. Loki, in Freyja's falcon cloak, finds Thrym sitting on a mound plaiting collars for his hounds, entirely pleased with himself: he has buried Mjollnir eight leagues deep and will return it only for Freyja as his bride. Freyja's refusal is so violent that the halls shake and her necklace snaps. Heimdall proposes dressing Thor as the bride instead, and Thor objects that the gods will call him unmanly until Loki points out that giants will otherwise be living in Asgard shortly. Veiled, Thor eats an ox, eight salmon and three casks of mead at the feast, and Loki explains each alarming detail away. When the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage, Thor takes it and kills everyone present.
entities.variantTraditions: Thrymskvida is one of the most polished poems in the Poetic Edda and reads as deliberate comedy; some scholars date it late for that reason.

entities.name: Angrboda
entities.role: Mother of the three monsters
symbols: the wolf, the serpent and the half-dead daughter
entities.bio: Loki's giantess consort, who bore Fenrir, Jormungandr and Hel.
entities.longBio: Angrboda's name means she who brings grief, and her entire significance is her three children by Loki: the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungandr, and Hel. The gods, learning of them and being told what they will do, act pre-emptively - Odin throws the serpent into the sea, sends Hel down to the world of the dead, and has the wolf raised among the gods until he grows too large to be safe. Every one of those three decisions is what makes the prophecy happen: the serpent grows to encircle the world, Hel rules the dead who will sail against them, and the wolf, betrayed and bound, kills Odin. Angrboda herself does nothing further in any surviving text.
entities.variantTraditions: She is named in the Poetic Edda only in passing; Snorri supplies the parentage of all three monsters.

entities.name: Surtr
entities.role: The fire-giant who burns the world
domains: the burning of the nine worlds
symbols: the flaming sword brighter than the sun
entities.bio: He has stood at the edge of the fire-world since before the beginning, waiting to burn everything at the end.
entities.longBio: Surtr is at the southern border of Muspelheim from the first moment, before the world exists, with a flaming sword, and he does nothing at all for the entire span of the mythology. At Ragnarok he rides out at the head of the sons of Muspell, the bridge Bifrost breaks under them as they cross, and he meets Freyr - who gave away his sword for Gerdr - and kills him. Then he flings fire over the whole earth and the nine worlds burn. He is not defeated by anyone; no god is assigned to him, and none survives him. Afterwards the earth rises green from the sea. He is one of the few figures in the tradition older than Ymir, and one of the very few who is not part of any family at all.
entities.variantTraditions: Icelandic place-names connect Surtr with volcanic features, and the 1963 eruption that created the island Surtsey was named for him.

entities.name: Mimir
entities.role: The head at the well of wisdom
domains: the knowledge under the world tree
entities.abode: Mimir's well, at a root of Yggdrasil
entities.bio: Odin gave an eye for one drink from his well, and later carried his severed head about for counsel.
entities.longBio: Mimir keeps a well at one of the roots of Yggdrasil in which wisdom and understanding are held, and he drinks from it every morning. Odin comes and asks for a draught; the price is an eye, which Odin pays without argument, and the eye lies in the well still. Mimir is later sent to the Vanir as a hostage in the truce alongside Hoenir. The arrangement fails - the Vanir conclude they have been cheated - and they cut off Mimir's head and send it back. Odin embalms it with herbs and speaks charms over it so that it can still talk, and afterwards consults it for counsel, particularly at moments of crisis. At the outbreak of Ragnarok he goes to speak with the head before anything else.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Mimir the well-keeper and Mimir the hostage are the same figure is not certain; the sources treat them as one without explaining how a beheaded hostage keeps a well.

entities.name: Aegir and Ran
entities.role: The sea-giant who brews for the gods, and his net-wielding wife
entities.abode: A hall beneath the sea, lit by gold
entities.bio: The sea personified as a host: he brews ale for the gods, and his wife drags the drowned down in her net.
entities.longBio: Aegir is the sea in its two aspects, and the tradition splits them between husband and wife. He is a genial host who brews ale for the gods in a mile-wide cauldron Thor fetches from the giant Hymir, and his hall is lit by gold laid on the floor rather than by fire, which is why poets call gold the fire of the sea. It is at his feast that Loki commits the outrage of Lokasenna, insulting every god present in turn. His wife Ran has a net, and she catches sailors and drags them down to her hall, where the drowned go; men carried gold to sea so as not to arrive at her hall empty-handed. Their nine daughters are the waves.
entities.variantTraditions: Aegir, Hler and Gymir may be three names for one being or three separate figures; the sources use them interchangeably in places.

entities.name: Hrungnir
entities.role: The stone-headed giant killed in the first duel
entities.bio: He raced Odin into Asgard, boasted drunkenly, and was killed by Thor in the tradition's set-piece duel.
entities.longBio: Odin, riding Sleipnir, wagers his head that no horse in Jotunheim can match him; Hrungnir's Gullfaxi keeps up so well that the giant rides straight through the gates of Asgard in pursuit. Offered hospitality, he drinks Thor's cups and announces he will carry off Valhalla, sink Asgard, kill all the gods and take Freyja and Sif home with him. Thor arrives. They arrange a formal duel, and the giants build a clay man nine leagues tall to stand with Hrungnir, into which they put a mare's heart, so it is terrified before anything begins. Hrungnir throws his whetstone; Thor throws Mjollnir; the two meet in the air, the hone shatters and a piece lodges in Thor's head, and the hammer kills the giant, whose leg falls across Thor and pins him.
entities.variantTraditions: The whetstone fragment stays in Thor's head, and Snorri uses it to explain why no one should throw a hone across a room.

entities.name: Utgarda-Loki
entities.role: The giant king who beat Thor with illusions
symbols: the enormous glove mistaken for a hall
entities.bio: He defeated Thor at three contests by disguising the sea, old age and thought as ordinary opponents.
entities.longBio: Thor, Loki and two servants reach a hall so vast they sleep in a side chamber, which turns out at dawn to be the thumb of a giant's glove. At Utgard the king sets contests. Loki loses an eating match to Logi. Thialfi loses a race to Hugi. Thor fails to empty a drinking horn, cannot lift a grey cat off the floor beyond one paw, and is wrestled to one knee by an old woman. As they leave, Utgarda-Loki tells them the truth and then vanishes with his castle: Logi was wildfire, Hugi was thought, the horn's other end was in the sea and Thor drank it down noticeably, the cat was the world serpent and he lifted it until the sky was touched, and the old woman was old age, whom no one has ever thrown.
entities.variantTraditions: The episode is Snorri's alone and is one of the finest pieces of narrative in the Prose Edda; no eddic poem preserves it.
